I służyć w jeździe, która wojuje szaraki,
Albo w piechocie, która nosi broń na ptaki,
Nie znać innych, prócz kosy i sierpa rynsztunków,
I innych gazet, oprócz domowych rachunków! . . .

Nad Soplicowem słońce weszło i już padło
Na strzechy i przez szpary w stodołę się wkradło;
I po ciemnozieloném, świeżém, wonném sianie,
Z którego młodzież sobie zrobiła posłanie,
Rozpływały się złote, migające pręgi
Z otworu czarnéj strzechy, jak z warkocza wstęgi;
I słońce usta sennych promykiem poranka
Drażni, jak dziewczę kłosem budzące kochanka.
Już wróble skacząc, świerkać zaczęły pod strzechą;
Już trzykroć gęgnął gąsior, a za nim jak echo,
Odezwały się chórem kaczki i indyki,
I słychać bydła w pole idącego ryki.

Wstała młodzież. Tadeusz jeszcze senny leży:
Bo też najpóźniej zasnął; z wczorajszéj wieczerzy
Wrócił tak niespokojny, że o kurów pianiu
Jeszcze oczu nie zmrużył, a na swém posłaniu
Tak kręcił się, że w siano jak w wodę utonął,
I spał twardo: aż zimny wiatr w oczy mu wionął,
Gdy skrzypiące stodoły drzwi otwarto z trzaskiem,
Bernardyn, ksiądz Robak, wszedł z węzlastym paskiem,
„Surge puer“ 1) wołając, i ponad barkami
Rubasznie wywijając pasek z ogórkami.

Już na dziedzińcu słychać myśliwskie okrzyki;
Wyprowadzają konie, zajeżdżają bryki,
Ledwie dziedziniec taką gromadę ogarnie.
Odezwały się trąby, otworzono psiarnie;
Grają chartów wypadłszy wesoło skowycze;
Widząc rumaki szczwaczów, dojeżdżaczów smycze,
Psy jak szalone cwałem śmigają po dworze;
Potém biegą i kładą szyje na obroże:
Wszystko to bardzo dobre polowanie wróży.

And to serve in the cavalry, which wages war on hares,
Or in the infantry, which bears arms against birds,
To know no other equipment but the scythe and the sickle,
And no other newspapers, except household accounts! . . .

Above Soplicowo the sun rose and already fell
Upon the thatch and crept into the barn through the gaps;
And over the dark green, fresh, fragrant hay,
From which the youth had made themselves a bed,
Gold, flickering ribbons dissolved
From the hole in the black thatch, like ribbons from a braid;
And the sun teases the lips of the sleepy with a ray of morning,
Like a girl waking her lover with an ear of wheat.
Already sparrows jumping, began to chirp under the thatch;
Already the gander honked thrice, and after it like an echo,
Ducks and turkeys replied in a chorus,
And the lowing of cattle going to the field is heard.

The youth rose. Tadeusz still lies sleepy:
For he also fell asleep the latest; from yesterday's supper
He returned so restless that at the crowing of the cocks
He had not yet closed his eyes, and on his bed
He twisted so that he sank into the hay as if into water,
And slept soundly: until a cold wind blew into his eyes,
When the creaking barn doors were opened with a crash,
The Bernardine, Father Robak, entered with a knotted belt,
Calling out <term>Surge puer</term> <gloss>get up, boy</gloss>, and swinging the belt with cucumbers <note>a humorous reference to the friar's humble, food-laden belt</note> over his shoulders in a coarse manner.

Already in the courtyard hunting cries are heard;
They lead out the horses, they harness the carriages,
The courtyard can barely hold such a throng.
Horns sounded, the kennels were opened;
The greyhounds play, having rushed out happily whimpering;
Seeing the steeds of the hunters and the leash-holders,
The dogs race like madmen at a gallop around the courtyard;
Then they run and place their necks into the collars:
All this bodes very good hunting.

Es ist klar, daß in dieser letzteren Bestimmung der eigentliche Zweck der Stiftung liegt: in der Form der Klostergründung, in Wahrheit ein sakral geschütztes, insbesondere, als Klostergut, gegen den Zugriff der weltlichen — und das hieß der patrimonial-bürokratischen — Gewalten geschütztes Familienfideikommiß mit voraussichtlich steigenden Einkünften. (Nebenher erreicht der Stifter noch den Zweck, das Wohlgefallen Gottes und der Menschen zu erringen und, unter Umständen, seiner Familie Einfluß auf die Besetzung der Mönchspründen und also Gelegenheit zu Gefälligkeiten an einflußreiche Familien — denn die Mönchspräbenden waren oft tatsächlich so gut wie pflichtlose Sinekuren für Konstantinopeler Garçons, da nicht nur Klausur, sondern auch Residenzpflicht fehlte — und auch Einfluß auf die Art der Verwaltung einer Familienkapelle zu sichern). Das ganze war eine Art von geldwirtschaftlichem Surrogat für das „Eigenkirchenwesen“ des feudalen Okzidents. Es scheint, daß Stiftungen in ganz ähnlicher Form schon unter der altägyptischen Patrimonialherrschaft vorkommen. Genau die gleiche Erscheinung findet sich jedenfalls im mittelalterlichen Islam als „Wakuf“ (Stiftung für Moscheen u. dgl.) wieder, wie es die Urkunden bezeugen. Und zwar wurden auch damals gerade Objekte, welche Geldwert, und zwar steigenden, tragen: Baugrund, Ergasterien (vermietbare Werkstätten) gestiftet, ganz ohne Zweifel zu dem gleichen Zweck und aus dem gleichen Grunde: weil die Weihe zum Kirchengut, wenn auch keine absolute Sicherheit, so doch das Optimum von Garantie gegen die willkürlichen Eingriffe der weltlichen Beamtenschaft bot. So wirkt die Willkür und Unberechenbarkeit der patrimonialen Herrschaft ihrerseits dahin, das Gebiet sakralrechtlicher Gebundenheit zu verstärken. Und da andererseits die theoretische Starrheit und Unabänderlichkeit der Scharî'a in ihrer subjektiven und oft ganz unberechenbaren Interpretation durch die Richter ihre „Korrektur“ fand, so steigerten sich die beiden der Entwicklung des Kapitalismus gleich feindlichen Bestandteile des Patrimonialismus gegenseitig. Denn daß die höchst nachhaltige Immobilisierung akkumulierten Besitzes in Gestalt der Wakufgebundenheit — ganz dem Geist der antiken Wirtschaft entsprechend, welche akkumuliertes Vermögen als Rentenfonds, nicht als Erwerbskapital benutzte — für die ökonomische Entwicklung des Orients von sehr großer Bedeutung gewesen ist, nimmt C. H. Becker sicher mit Recht an. (Durch spanische Vermittlung ist dann das, wahrscheinlich eine säkularisierte Nachbildung des Wakuf bildende, Institut des profanen „Fideikommisses“, welches dort zuerst auftaucht, im 17. Jahrhundert nach Deutschland importiert worden.) —

Und endlich war dem Patrimonialismus gerade auf dem Boden einer relativ entwickelten Geldwirtschaft und speziell in Epochen, wo er sich einem rationalen bürokratischen System stark annähert, noch eine Art der Einwirkung auf die ökonomische Entwicklung eigen, die aus der Form seiner Bedarfsdeckung folgte. Wie der „Patrimonialstaat“ sich leicht in ein Bündel von Privilegien auflöste, so lag ihm auch einerseits die monopolistisch-erwerbswirtschaftliche, andererseits die privilegierende Bedarfsdeckung (im früher besprochenen Sinn des Wortes) besonders nahe. Mit Hilfe eines gut funktionierenden Patrimonialbeamtentums ließen sich alle Arten fiskalischer Unternehmungen und Monopole besonders leicht durchführen. Sowohl der ägyptische wie der spätrömische Staat und die Staaten des nahen und fernen Ostens haben in teilweise sehr umfassender Weise Staatsbetriebe geschaffen und auch Monopole ausnutzt, und die Regiegewerbe von Fürsten der beginnenden Neuzeit liegen in dieser Richtung. Die erwerbswirtschaftliche öffentliche Bedarfsdeckung ist keineswegs auf den Patrimonialismus beschränkt geblieben: auch die Kommunen haben im Mittelalter und im Beginn der Neuzeit sich, oft mit großen Verlusten (so Frankfurt a. M.), auch an recht gewagten gewerblichen oder Handelsunternehmungen von reinem Erwerbscharakter beteiligt. It is clear that the actual purpose of the foundation lies in this latter provision: it is, in the form of a monastery founding, in truth a family trust <term>Familienfideikommiß</term> <gloss>entail</gloss> protected in a sacred manner, specifically protected as monastery property against the seizure of worldly—and that meant patrimonial-bureaucratic—powers, with presumably increasing income. (Incidentally, the founder also achieves the goal of gaining the pleasure of God and men and, under certain circumstances, of securing for his family influence on the occupation of the monastic prebends and thus the opportunity for favors to influential families—for the monastic prebends were often in fact as good as duty-free sinecures for Constantinople's bachelors, since not only cloister life but also the obligation of residence was missing—and also influence on the manner of the administration of a family chapel). The whole thing was a kind of money-economic substitute for the "proprietary church system" <term>Eigenkirchenwesen</term> <gloss>system where a landlord owns the church on his land</gloss> of the feudal Occident. It seems that foundations in a very similar form already occurred under ancient Egyptian patrimonial rule. Exactly the same phenomenon is found in any case in the medieval Islam as "Wakuf" (foundation for mosques and the like) again, as the documents testify. And indeed, even then, objects that carry monetary value, and specifically increasing value, were endowed: construction land, <term>ergasteria</term> <gloss>rentable workshops</gloss>, without a doubt for the same purpose and for the same reason: because the consecration as church property, even if it offered no absolute security, nonetheless offered the optimum of guarantee against the arbitrary interventions of the worldly bureaucracy. Thus, the arbitrariness and unpredictability of patrimonial rule acts in its turn to strengthen the area of sacred-legal boundedness. And since, on the other hand, the theoretical rigidity and immutability of the <term>Scharî'a</term> <gloss>Islamic religious law</gloss> found its "correction" in its subjective and often quite unpredictable interpretation by the judges, the two components of patrimonialism that are equally hostile to the development of capitalism mutually intensified one another. For C. H. Becker is certainly correct in assuming that the highly lasting immobilization of accumulated property in the form of Wakuf-binding—entirely in accordance with the spirit of the ancient economy, which used accumulated wealth as a rent fund, not as acquisition capital—has been of very great importance for the economic development of the Orient. (Through Spanish mediation, the institution of the profane "entail," which likely forms a secularized imitation of the Wakuf and which first appears there, was then imported into Germany in the 17th century.) —

And finally, patrimonialism, precisely on the soil of a relatively developed money economy and especially in epochs where it strongly approaches a rational bureaucratic system, possessed yet another type of influence on economic development, which followed from the form of its supply fulfillment. Just as the "patrimonial state" easily dissolved into a bundle of privileges, so too was it particularly inclined, on the one hand, to monopolistic-acquisitive and, on the other, to preferential supply fulfillment (in the sense of the word discussed earlier). With the help of a well-functioning patrimonial civil service, all kinds of fiscal enterprises and monopolies could be carried out particularly easily. Both the Egyptian and the late Roman state, as well as the states of the Near and Far East, created state-run enterprises in a partially very comprehensive manner and also utilized monopolies, and the state-run businesses of princes of the early modern period lie in this direction. That everyone who died and made that descent,
He has regret for the transition and death,
But it is a regret for the lack of fulfillment.
Whoever dies, he has a body,

From greed, there is little contentment,
And from fear, there is little humility in that face.
Likewise, from greed, there is little in the mountain,
And from Iblis, there is good prostration in the face.
Do not pluck the feather that adorns the paradise,
Do not pluck the veil that measures.
When he heard this advice and realized the gratitude,
After that, he began to cry in a new way.
Lamentation and crying from the pain-stricken,
Whoever was there was thrown into his crying.
And the one who was asking about plucking the feather,
Became without answer, ashamed, and mourning.
"Why did I foolishly ask him?"
"He is full of his own grief, in a state of agitation."
Water dripped from his wet eyes,
In every drop, a hundred answers were contained.
Crying with sincerity strikes the soul,
Until it makes the heavens and the throne cry.
The intellect and the hearts that are of the Throne,
Are in a veil, striking from the light of the Throne.

### On the explanation that the intellect and the spirit are imprisoned in water and clay like Harut and Marut in the well of Babel

Like Harut and Marut, those two pure ones,
They are bound here in a fearsome well.
The world of intellect and appetite is within,
Within this well, until they are bound by the crime.
Magic and anti-magic, without choice,
From these two, the good and the wicked learn.
But take that bad advice as a guide,
Do not learn magic, and do not collect it.
"We teach magic," says the other,
"For the sake of trial and examination."
"Condition is required for the test,"
"You have no choice without power."
Desires are like sleeping dogs,
Within them, good and evil are hidden.
Since there is no power, these ten have slept,
Like a name on a foot or a body.
Until a carrion comes in between,
The mystery of the images of greed, what was it in the mine?
When a carrion donkey died in that alley,
A hundred sleeping dogs were awakened by it.
Greeds went into the treasure of the unseen,
Bringing an attack and striking at the pocket.

*A. AURICOMUS*, smaller, thinner, with a yellowish pileus, striate margin, a fistulose stipe, and affixed, ventricose, whitish-brown lamellae. *Batsch. f. 21.* On burned ground, to be separated from the yellowish-stemmed *A. geophyllus*, strikingly rimose.

701. *A. PERBREVIS*, with a subfleshy, convex, obtusely umbonate, longitudinally fibrous or squamose pileus, with a substriate margin, finally fissured, a stuffed, short, pale, white-fibrillose stipe, slightly attenuated at the base, and uncinate-adnexed, subdistant, whitish-brownish or argillaceous lamellae. *Weinm. p. 185. A. ereus. Secr. n. 304.* In broad-leaved woods, rare. Small, but rather firm, brownish or reddish-yellow, stipe barely an inch, cortinate, opaque, pruinose at the apex. Flesh white.

702. *A. HIULCUS*, with a subfleshy, conical-expanded, umbonate, fibrillose, rimose-squamose pileus, a stuffed, rigid, elongated, silky-fibrillose stipe, white-pruinose at the apex and white-fleshed, and subfree, barely crowded, broad, white-fleshed lamellae, darker at the base, finally olivaceous. *Batt. t. 18. C.!* — *A. lacerus Secr. n. 318, 319* also seem to be here. On pine forest ground. Odor, to me, abounding in sneezing powder, obsolete. Stipe 2—3 inches long, 2 lines thick, slightly curved, equal, with a bulbillose base. Pileus brown, olive.

703. *A. GRATUS*, with a subfleshy, conical-campanulate, fibrillose pileus, expanded, rimose, umbonate, with a darker squamose disc, a stuffed, shiny, fibrillose, flexuous, white-reddish stipe, and adnexed, crowded, thin, olive-pale to brownish lamellae. *Weinm.! p. 185. — Secr. n. 311*, who leads *Bull. t. 522. f. 2* here not without veracity of the species. In grassy places. It approaches *A. geophyllus* or *A. scabellus* rather closely, easily distinct by its pleasant anise odor. Pileus whitish or yellowish-reddish. Stipe obsoletely pruinose at the apex. (v. s.)

704. *A. TRINII*, with a subfleshy, hemispherical, obtuse, longitudinally reddish-fibrillose pileus, a stuffed, equal, slender, loosely red-fibrillose, white-farinaceous stipe, and rounded, ventricose, cinnamon lamellae, white-flocculose at the edge. *Weinm.! p. 194.* In grassy broad-leaved woods. At Saint Petersburg! Rare, significant, heteroclitic! with a carnation odor. Pileus barely rimose, nor squamose, ½ inch, whitish-reddish, tawny when dry.
